name: NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001
question: How do we run AI governance as a system, not a scramble?
summary: The NIST AI Risk Management Framework organises AI risk work into Govern, Map, Measure and Manage, with a Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1) for LLM-specific risks. ISO/IEC 42001:2023 is a certifiable AI management system standard: policy, risk and impact assessment, controls, competence, operation, internal audit and management review. Neither is Indian law, but both give a structure that makes RBI, SEBI, DPDP and EU evidence repeatable, and one well-built control usually satisfies several frameworks.
useCases: Building a governance programme from scratch
Clients or partners asking for certification
Mapping one set of controls to several regulations

steps.title: Pick a backbone
steps.text: NIST AI RMF for risk practice, ISO/IEC 42001 when clients want a certificate. Many banks use both.

steps.title: One control, many mappings
steps.text: Each control lists every framework and clause it serves. An AI policy counts for NIST Govern, ISO 5.2, RBI’s policy recommendation and the EU quality system.

steps.title: Map: assess impact per use case
steps.text: An impact assessment for each AI use is NIST’s Map function and ISO 42001’s AI system impact assessment; ISO/IEC 42005 gives guidance.

steps.title: Measure and Manage need engineering
steps.text: Eval suites, red teaming, monitoring and incident runbooks from Panels 1, 11 and 12 are the evidence behind these functions.

steps.title: Measure coverage per framework
steps.text: Coverage shows where one library falls short for a given regulator, instead of starting a new project.

steps.title: Audit and review on a schedule
steps.text: Internal audit and management review keep the system alive. The bank cut evidence requests from 400 items to 150.

practice.scenario: A private bank’s governance team was running four separate checklists: RBI expectations, DPDP, an ISO/IEC 42001 request from a corporate client, and the EU AI Act for its London and Frankfurt desks. It replaced them with one library of 38 controls, each mapped to every framework it served. Evidence requests from auditors fell from about 400 items to 150, because one eval report or incident runbook now answered several frameworks at once.

practice.note: The clause references are simplified for illustration; confirm mappings against the standards and regulations before relying on them.

samples.code:
CONTROLS = {
    "ai_policy":        {"NIST": ["GOVERN"], "ISO42001": ["5.2"], "RBI": ["policy"], "EU": ["QMS"]},
    "ai_inventory":     {"NIST": ["GOVERN", "MAP"], "ISO42001": ["6.1"], "RBI": ["inventory"]},
    "impact_assessment":{"NIST": ["MAP"], "ISO42001": ["6.1.4"], "EU": ["risk management", "FRIA"]},
    "eval_suite":       {"NIST": ["MEASURE"], "ISO42001": ["8"], "RBI": ["validation"], "EU": ["accuracy"]},
    "red_teaming":      {"NIST": ["MEASURE"], "EU": ["robustness"]},
    "monitoring":       {"NIST": ["MEASURE", "MANAGE"], "ISO42001": ["9.1"], "EU": ["post-market monitoring"]},
    "incident_runbook": {"NIST": ["MANAGE"], "ISO42001": ["10.2"], "RBI": ["incident"], "EU": ["serious incidents"]},
    "vendor_review":    {"NIST": ["GOVERN", "MANAGE"], "ISO42001": ["A.10"], "RBI": ["third party"]},
}

def coverage(implemented: set, framework: str, required: set) -> float:
    met = set()
    for c in implemented:
        met.update(CONTROLS.get(c, {}).get(framework, []))
    return len(met & required) / len(required)

print(coverage({"ai_policy", "eval_suite", "incident_runbook"},
               "NIST", {"GOVERN", "MAP", "MEASURE", "MANAGE"}))     # 0.75

numericDrill.question: A bank replaced four separate compliance checklists with one control library, cutting auditor evidence requests from 400 items to 150. By what percentage did the evidence requests fall?
numericDrill.answer: (400 − 150) ÷ 400 = 62.5%. The saving comes from mapping each control, such as one eval report or one incident runbook, to every framework it satisfies, so it is produced once and cited many times.

interview.question: How do the NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001 differ?
interview.answer: The NIST AI RMF is a voluntary framework organised into Govern, Map, Measure and Manage, with profiles such as the Generative AI Profile; it guides what to do but is not certifiable. ISO/IEC 42001 is a management-system standard with requirements and Annex A controls that an accredited body can certify, which clients often ask for. Many organisations use NIST for risk practice and ISO 42001 for the certifiable system.

interview.question: Why use a framework if no Indian law requires it?
interview.answer: Because regulators ask for evidence of governance, not for a particular framework. A framework gives a repeatable structure, avoids a separate project per regulation, and lets one well-built control satisfy RBI, SEBI, DPDP and EU expectations at once.
